title: Antigone
author: Sophocles
openingText: ANTIGONE and ISMENE before the Palace gates.
about:
Eteocles and Polynices have killed each other in the struggle for Thebes. Their uncle Creon is now king. He orders an honourable burial for Eteocles but forbids anyone to bury Polynices, who attacked the city. Antigone decides to defy the order and bury her brother.

The conflict spreads through their family and the city. Ismene fears the consequences of her sister's decision, Haemon tries to persuade his father to listen, and the seer Tiresias warns of divine anger. The chorus relates the action to human achievement, the power of love and the family's inherited suffering.

This modern version follows Francis Storr's English translation, with selected corrections checked against the Greek text. Its modern wording does not reproduce the original metre.

angleCards.title: Who has authority over the dead?
angleCards.text: Antigone invokes the gods' unwritten laws; Creon defends his authority as ruler. Follow their reasons for demanding obedience and the links between burial, family, religion and politics.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine their arguments and how the events of the play test them.

angleCards.title: Listening and yielding
angleCards.text: Haemon uses trees in a flood and a ship in a storm to explain why yielding can be wise. Notice when Creon treats advice as a personal attack.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Creon's response to disagreement and understand why he changes his decision.

angleCards.title: The sisters' choices
angleCards.text: Ismene initially refuses to help with the burial but later wants to share the blame. Antigone rejects her offer. Their exchanges suggest different understandings of love, fear and responsibility.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare the sisters without deciding in advance that one is brave and the other cowardly.

angleCards.title: The changing chorus
angleCards.text: The chorus comments, questions and advises. Read its songs about humanity and love alongside the characters' decisions.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to notice when the chorus supports authority, hesitates or revises its judgment.

cast.name: Antigone
cast.role: The sister who defies the order
cast.description: Oedipus' daughter and sister of Eteocles, Polynices and Ismene. She buries Polynices and openly defends her action. She is engaged to Haemon.

cast.name: Ismene
cast.description: She fears the king's power and initially refuses to help. When Antigone is accused, she wants to share her guilt and fate.

cast.name: Creon
cast.description: Antigone's uncle and Haemon's father. He forbids Polynices' burial and treats opposition as a threat to his authority.

cast.name: Haemon
cast.description: Antigone's betrothed. He tells his father what citizens are saying privately and urges him to listen to others.

cast.name: Tiresias
cast.description: He reports that sacrificial signs have failed because birds and dogs have carried remains of the unburied body to the altars. His warning becomes decisive.

cast.name: The Chorus
cast.description: The chorus follows the conflict, sings about its wider implications and offers advice. Its responses shift as events unfold.

whyItMatters.title: Law and conscience
whyItMatters.body: The play makes conflicting duties concrete through a body, a burial and a death sentence. It invites questions about what justifies a law and when obedience becomes wrong.

whyItMatters.title: Conviction and grief
whyItMatters.body: Antigone maintains her decision but also mourns the life and marriage she will lose. Her lament lets readers consider her certainty alongside her vulnerability.

whyItMatters.title: Responsibility recognised too late
whyItMatters.body: Creon eventually changes course but cannot undo the consequences of his decisions. The ending connects judgment with listening and the limits of human power.
